title: Stop-the-World: The Janitor's Method
concept: When GC runs, the program pauses briefly. This is called 'Stop-the-World', and minimizing this pause time is the core goal of GC algorithms.

steps.title: main Method Starts
steps.explanation:
**`public static void main(String[] args)`**

The program's entry point.
We'll observe the 'pause phenomenon' that occurs when GC runs.

steps.title: Normal Execution
steps.explanation:
The program is running normally.
The CPU is busy doing work.

steps.title: Freeze! (Stop-the-World)
steps.explanation:
For memory cleanup (GC), **all threads freeze and stop.**
It's like when the janitor is waxing the floor -- nobody is allowed to walk through.

steps.title: Unfreeze! (Execution Resumes)
steps.explanation:
Once cleanup is done, the frozen tasks resume and continue running.
If this pause lasts too long, users perceive it as "lag".

quiz.question: What is the phenomenon called when the JVM pauses application execution for GC?
quiz.explanation: The phenomenon where all threads except the GC thread are paused is called Stop-the-World (STW).

misconceptions.wrong: With GC, you don't need to worry about memory at all.
misconceptions.correct: Not true! For GC to clean up properly, you need to make objects 'unreferenced'.
misconceptions.why: If you unknowingly keep references to unused objects, even the janitor can't clean them up.

keyTakeaway: The evolution of GC algorithms has been driven by the goal of minimizing STW pause times.
